Encyclopédie des nouveaux usages des collections dans les musées d’art
Acquisition
Encyclopedia of New Uses of Collections

item.hi: Josée Drouin-Brisebois, Producer and Senior Management, National Outreach, National Gallery of Canada
Jessica Minier, PhD Candidate, Université du Québec en Outaouais

p.hi: Museums today are showing ingenuity in continuing to develop their collections while working with limited resources and purchasing power. As the art market is characterised by a limited supply of works, this results in strong demand, generating competition both between the private and public sectors, as well as among museums themselves. In an ‘age of access’ (Rifkin, 2000), joint acquisition is proliferating as a form of collaborative musealization. Joint acquisition is a new modality of musealization whose origins go back to the 1970s. The very first identified case occurred in 1973, when the Metropolitan Museum of Art (MET) and the Louvre jointly acquired an ivory comb depicting the Tree of Jesse, dating from the early 13th century (Shirey, 1973). In the past decade, there has been an acceleration in joint acquisitions. Since 2010, there has been a significant increase in joint acquisitions, reaching a number comparable to that recorded between 1973 and 2010. Despite this growing professional interest, joint acquisition remains a relatively unexplored subject in museological studies. Shared ownership between museums is mentioned in certain reference works (Matassa, 2010, 2011; Tobelem, 2023) and was the subject of a master's thesis (van Ravenzwaay, University of Amsterdam, 2015). Since joint acquisition has not been the subject of in-depth research in the French-speaking museum community, this entry establishes its theoretical foundations.

It consists of the receipt or acceptance of one or more objects into the collections. According to the Société des musées du Québec, acquisition is defined as “the activity through which an object or group of objects legally becomes the property of the museum institution and is incorporated into its collections” (translated from the French; Société des musées du Québec, 2016). In addition to reducing acquisition costs for all partners in the case of a joint purchase, co-acquisition increases access to the work: on one hand, for the public, who can view it in different locations, and on the other hand, for the co-owners, who can each present, document, and study it (Matassa, 2011). Since works are part of more than one collection at a time, they are assigned an acquisition number in each institution (ARCS, n.d.). These institutions, which already share ownership, also share authority over decisions concerning the co-acquired work. Every joint acquisition is accompanied by a “protocol” (Bergeron, 2022) that outlines the rights and obligations of the co-owners. This agreement specifies the number of works involved, as well as the terms of purchase (if applicable), ownership and possession, conservation, loan to third parties, reproduction, sale, insurance and indemnification, documentation and research, storage, access, and transportation (ARCS, n.d.; National Gallery of Canada, 2018). If the shared work is a physical object, usage time must be divided, as well as transportation and handling costs. Additional considerations include storage, potential loans, conservation, and restoration of the work. In general, digital works, which can exist in multiple copies across various media, facilitate sharing, as insurance for transportation is not always necessary and the risks to the work are lower (Kaufman, 2004).

Joint acquisition takes many forms: the types of partners, the methods of joint acquisition, and the sharing models are varied. While it can make several museum institutions co-owners, co-acquisition can also give rise to other types of partnerships. Joint acquisition agreements have been concluded between departments within the same museum; between museums and archives, documentation, and research centres; between museums and foundations; between museums and private collections; between museums and donors; between museums and individuals; between museums and universities; and between museums and municipal councils (or cities).

For institutions with a collection, joint acquisition allows the addition of one or more works to institutional collections through various means, such as purchase and donation. On one hand, joint purchase involves sharing the acquisition price, whether equally or not among the parties involved. In some cases, it results from collaborative exhibitions between museums or gallery initiatives. On the other hand, co-acquisition occurs when a donor chooses to give a work simultaneously to multiple institutions. If a donation is defined as “the legal act through which a donor transfers ownership of property free of charge to the museum” (translated from the French; Mairesse, 2022), a donation to more than one institution necessarily entails both transfer and shared ownership. To date, this type of donation has been made in art museums by private collectors and by an artist. The

, a practice popular in the United States at the beginning of the century due to a legal loophole, is another form of donation leading to shared ownership of a work between a donor and a museum. It allowed a collector to donate a work gradually, a strategy that culminated in a bequest (Follas, 2008). Alternatively, co-acquisition can be the culmination of programmes set up for commissioning contemporary works accompanied by a promise of acquisition in multiple collections.

Finally, the terms of property sharing also vary from one joint acquisition to another; three models have been identified so far. The most common model is equal sharing of both acquisition costs, in the case of a joint purchase, and ultimately of the work itself. Co-owners therefore hold equal shares, which guarantees them the same type of access and the same usage time. Not only are each party’s rights symmetrical, but so are their obligations toward the work. In some cases, the sharing is based on a ratio reflecting the financial contribution of the parties involved in a joint purchase. Thus, a larger museum may pay a higher amount than its partner, which could entitle it to negotiate increased access to the work. In this specific case, the co-owners’ rights and obligations are asymmetrical. Finally, an alternative that blends the two models is also possible: a larger museum may cover a larger portion of the acquisition costs and then share the work equally with the other co-owners.

Until recently, museums were little concerned with the size of their collections or the practical aspects of their conservation (Office of Policy and Analysis, 2003). Throughout the 20th century, many museums acquired as much as possible within their collecting scope. Collections, often large, lacked cohesion and sometimes contained objects that did not meet museum-quality standards (Office of Policy and Analysis, 2003). From the last quarter of the 20th century onwards, greater attention has been paid to the consequences of collecting practices, a concern that has grown in importance since the 1990s. This shift was driven in part by declining government and philanthropic support coupled with economic slowdowns, a lack of storage space in full reserves leading to refusals, museums’ inability to catch up on collection processing, and the general shift of collection priorities toward exhibitions and public programming (Office of Policy and Analysis, 2003). As a result, museums began exploring new approaches to acquisitions (Office of Policy and Analysis, 2003). The desire to develop collections more sustainably and the need to reduce costs should encourage museum professionals to view resource sharing as an opportunity to contribute to the cultural life of a community (Matassa, 2010).

In this respect, joint acquisition represents a sustainable avenue for developing collections while also ensuring a sharing of costs and responsibility for care, particularly regarding storage and conservation (Matassa, 2011). Indeed, when two or more museums have co-acquired a physical work, only one museum at a time needs to store and conserve the object, providing the other museum with space in its storage. This is a significant advantage, as many storage facilities are overburdened due to museums’ accumulation logic, which contrasts with deaccessioning (van Ravenzwaay, 2015).
Addressing Scarcity in the Art Market

Joint acquisition helps address the scarcity of works in the highly competitive markets for established and contemporary art. Firstly, the market for established art, which includes works of historical heritage, is characterised by limited supply, increasing rarity, and artistic values validated over time, history, and social consensus (Moulin, 2009). In this market of scarcity, museums do not always have the financial resources to acquire works by sought-after artists. Museum administrations are therefore compelled to structure financial arrangements involving patronage in order to maintain purchasing power (Moulin, 2009) or to pursue co-acquisitions. Secondly, scarcity operates differently in the contemporary art market. As contemporary artists are generally still alive, supply is ongoing. In addition, new technologies, which allow for the multiplication of works and challenge the very foundations of the market, stimulate mechanisms to recreate scarcity and enhance economic value (Moulin, 2009). Moreover, new media works often encourage a philosophy of sharing in their conservation rather than exclusive ownership (Park, 2017). Considering that real or perceived scarcity affects the value of works, joint acquisition allows museums that pool their resources to shape gallery sales, ensuring that art remains accessible to them (van Ravenzwaay, 2015). In a globalised art market, it also allows gallery owners to strategically distribute editions of a work across collections worldwide, providing international visibility for their artists. Through joint acquisition, museums maintain their position in the art market, preventing works from being confined solely to the private sphere (van Ravenzwaay, 2015).
Increasing the Fundraising Capacity of the Museum

Beyond competition in the art market, museums also compete for funding. Their proliferation worldwide in recent decades has put them in competition for grants, private donations, and ticket revenues (Nicolas and Ginsburgh, 2022). Once again, museum institutions benefit from collaborating on acquisitions, sharing funding rather than competing for it. Joint acquisition, which promotes responsible use of resources, cost reduction, and the retention of artworks in the public sector, can also enhance museums’ fundraising capacity (Matassa, 2011; van Ravenzwaay, 2015). On one hand, museums can solicit their donors, each drawing on their network, and the funds collected are then used to acquire the desired work. On the other hand, museums engaging in joint acquisition can benefit from specific grants. For example, in the UK, the Heritage Lottery Fund and the Art Fund are both dedicated to improving access to art, and encourage co-ownership as it ensures the retention of important works within the country (van Ravenzwaay, 2015).

Often, the threat of a work being sold into the private sphere—especially abroad—motivates a group of museums to purchase it “for the nation” (Matassa, 2011). Past cultural heritage exodus has led several countries to protect it through export control systems in a retentionist approach (Palanco, 2018). Generally, three criteria guide the granting of an export licence: (1) the work’s connection to national history or life; (2) its aesthetic importance; and (3) its significance for the study of a particular branch of art (Serota, 2005). The first criterion concerns works created within the nation or constituting a notable testimony of social, political, economic, or cultural history, based on the principle that objects have greater meaning and value when seen in the context of their creation (Serota, 2005). While there is no intention to prohibit a masterpiece by French, Italian, or British artists, for example, from leaving the country, a conservation instinct naturally arises when a work comes from a historic collection or maintains a historical link to the nation. When a work has been kept in a private house and remained unknown or little known for generations, there is a tendency to use its market availability to enrich a regional or national collection (Serota, 2005). When a work associated with a nation risks leaving its territory, joint acquisition can become a retention strategy for museums, from which an urgent action is required. Collaborative acquisition allows resources to be pooled quickly, preventing export.

While national public collections reflect the identity of a community—local, regional, national, or international in the case of so-called “universal” museums (Serota, 2005)—placing artistic heritage in public collections abroad can help a nation gain international recognition. However, the logistics involved are complex, given the instinct for heritage retention. Initially, export controls aimed to protect cultural heritage by preventing illicit import, export, and transfer of ownership. States adhering to the Convention on the Means of Prohibiting and Preventing the Illicit Import, Export and Transfer of Ownership of Cultural Property (1970) had to adopt protective measures domestically and control the movement of cultural property (UNESCO, 2022). These measures include the issuance of an export certificate required for any temporary or permanent removal from the territory. In the case of a national treasure—a work belonging to public collections, classified, or of major national heritage interest—removal can only be temporary (Gouvernement de la République française [Government of the French Republic], 2022). Temporary removals are authorised for restoration, appraisal, participation in a cultural event, exhibition, or deposit in a public collection only (Gouvernement de la République française [Government of the French Republic], 2022). If a work is put up for public auction but obtaining an export certificate is not feasible, joint acquisition can serve as a workaround. Consequently, the work can maintain a connection with its country of origin through the presence of one of the co-owning museums; temporary shuttles between countries may then be organised.

Joint acquisition contributes to the circulation of collections, evoking the notion of a network. In the 1960s, the art world and art museums shifted from a “system” ideology to a “network” one, characterised notably by the circulation and mobility of works (Relya, 2013). In this sense, joint acquisition encourages movement of collections between institutions, promoting better access as well as sharing of knowledge and expertise. Because joint acquisition involves extended display time through exhibitions in partner museums (van Ravenzwaay, 2015), works spend less time in storage. Access to the work is multiplied both by the number of display locations and by the longer exhibition period. The public benefits from joint acquisition, particularly as it meets the need for frequent renewal of collection displays (van Ravenzwaay, 2015). However, depending on the medium, joint acquisitions may require more frequent transportation, with all associated risks (van Ravenzwaay, 2015). Moreover, museums are encouraged to engage in research to understand the origins and nature of their collections, enabling enriched use (Petterson, 2010). In this respect, joint acquisition involves not one, but multiple teams, all of whom have access to the work. Joint acquisition encourages further research on collections while fostering cooperation among researchers, potentially leading to knowledge exchange (van Ravenzwaay, 2015).

The ethics of exclusion gives way to an ethics of inclusion, as equity enters the artistic tradition (Fred and Farrell, 2008). Collecting practices are being reassessed through the lens of equality, diversity, and indigeneity as art museums engage in decolonisation. This openness aims to expand the conventional artistic repertoire (Fred and Farrell, 2008), which traditionally promoted a white male identity (Pollock, 2007), and to increase diversity in collections. In this context, joint acquisition can become a strategy to acquire works at lower costs, thereby broadening the museum’s collecting scope and diversifying collections more rapidly. Joint acquisition thus allows museums to embrace cultural diversity (Grams and Farrell, 2008), address gaps in past acquisitions, and increase the representativeness of their collections. While these outcomes seem laudable, it is important to note that museums simultaneously compete for works by white male artists at very high market prices. One might assume that museums benefit from a bargain when jointly acquiring works by diverse artists. However, by recognising gaps in their collections and seeking to fill them, museums as “

” (“prescribers”; Moulin, 2009) create strong demand for works by Indigenous or diverse artists, whether historical or contemporary. Given the limited supply of historical works, joint acquisition is a strategy used by museums to enable diversification of their collections.
Increasing the “Cultural Capital” of a Smaller Institution

Although generally not perceived this way, museums can act as true “predators” in collection acquisition (Maranda and Soares, 2017). They behave this way when competing with other museums for works or seeking exclusive ownership of an object (Park, 2017). However, in joint acquisitions, museums act more as partners than rivals (Park, 2017). In some cases, larger institutions even assist smaller ones. This is notably the case with the National Gallery of Canada, which considers joint acquisition if it allows “extending its influence and assisting other institutions” (translated from the French;

head.hi: In conclusion, co-acquisition, initially introduced on a case-by-case basis in museums, appears to be normalising and extending beyond purely economic or heritage motivations. The contexts in which co-ownership arises are varied: sometimes partnerships emerge from particular circumstances, sometimes from a proposal by an external actor, and other times they are carefully planned. Depending on the nature of the partnership, engagement differs regarding the sharing of resources, knowledge, and expertise. In short, the transformative potential of joint acquisition is relative: for some museums, it seems to catalyse change, while for others, it appears to support the maintenance of the status quo.
